stem: A 19-year-old man with acute lymphoblastic leukemia has had an absolute neutrophil count below 500/mm3 for a month during induction chemotherapy. He now has fever, pleuritic chest pain and a lower-lobe infiltrate with an effusion. The pleural fluid shows thin hyphae that branch at acute angles and have septa. Bacterial cultures are negative.
oneliner: 19M + ALL + neutropenia for 1 mo + fever, pleuritic pain, infiltrate, effusion + septate hyphae branching at acute angles → which drug?
ask: Which of the following drugs is most appropriate?

whyNot.B: **Carbapenem** for bacteria; cultures are negative and fungi are seen
whyNot.E: **Topical or swallowed only**; not absorbed, so useless for lung infection

why: **Long neutropenia + septate hyphae branching at acute angles** = invasive aspergillosis. Choose a mold-active drug: **amphotericin B** among these options (voriconazole is the usual first choice).

drug.name: Amphotericin B
drug.how: Binds ergosterol and makes pores in the fungal membrane
drug.use: Serious systemic fungal infections (Cryptococcus with flucytosine, Mucor, Aspergillus)
drug.watch: Nephrotoxicity, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, infusion fever and chills

stem: A 15-year-old girl was treated 6 months ago for rheumatic fever. At that time she had migratory polyarthritis, subcutaneous nodules and a new apical murmur 3 weeks after a sore throat. The murmur persists, and echocardiography shows mild mitral regurgitation. She has no drug allergies. A long-term regimen is planned to prevent further attacks.
oneliner: 15F + rheumatic fever 6 mo ago (migratory arthritis, nodules, new murmur) + mild MR persists + no allergies → which drug to prevent recurrence?
ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term prophylaxis?

whyNot.A: No role in preventing recurrent **group A streptococcal** rheumatic fever
whyNot.B: Does not reliably eradicate **group A strep** pharyngitis
whyNot.E: Poor **streptococcal** coverage; not used for prophylaxis

why: **Migratory arthritis + nodules + carditis after sore throat** = acute rheumatic fever. **Penicillin** prevents recurrent group A strep infection; prophylaxis is given as **monthly IM benzathine penicillin G**, for years because of carditis.

drug.name: Benzathine penicillin G
drug.how: Binds penicillin-binding proteins; blocks peptidoglycan cross-linking
drug.use: Rheumatic fever prophylaxis, syphilis, group A strep pharyngitis
drug.watch: Hypersensitivity, injection-site pain, Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction in syphilis; give IM only

stem: A 17-year-old girl at 16 weeks of gestation has mucopurulent cervical discharge and a friable cervix. A nucleic acid amplification test is positive for Chlamydia trachomatis and negative for Neisseria gonorrhoeae. She has no drug allergies. A single-dose oral treatment that is safe for the fetus is chosen.
oneliner: 17F + 16 wk pregnant + mucopurulent discharge, friable cervix + chlamydia NAAT positive, gonorrhea negative + no allergies → which drug?
ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

whyNot.B: Standard in non-pregnant patients but **stains fetal bone and teeth**; avoided in pregnancy
whyNot.C: Treats **gonorrhea**, not chlamydia; gonorrhea test here is negative
whyNot.D: Risk of **gray baby syndrome**; not used for chlamydia
whyNot.E: **Folate antagonist** with teratogenic and kernicterus risk; not for chlamydia

why: **Chlamydia in pregnancy**: **doxycycline** is avoided because tetracyclines **stain fetal bone and teeth**. **Azithromycin** is the safe single-dose choice.

drug.name: Azithromycin
drug.how: Binds the 50S ribosomal subunit and blocks translocation
drug.use: Chlamydia (including in pregnancy), community-acquired pneumonia, pertussis, MAC prophylaxis
drug.watch: QT prolongation, GI upset, cholestatic hepatitis; fewer CYP3A4 interactions than erythromycin

stem: A 41-year-old man with AIDS is brought to the ICU with 3 days of fever, confusion and a blood pressure of 82/50 mm Hg. Blood cultures grow encapsulated yeast that stain with mucicarmine, and serum cryptococcal antigen is strongly positive. CSF opening pressure is elevated.
oneliner: 41M + AIDS + fever, confusion, hypotension + blood culture mucicarmine-positive yeast + high CSF pressure → best initial drug?
ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate drug for induction therapy?

whyNot.A: **Fluconazole**: fungistatic; used for consolidation and lifelong maintenance, not for a critically ill induction
whyNot.D: **Terbinafine**: dermatophyte drug; not for systemic infection
whyNot.E: **Nystatin**: topical or swish-and-swallow only, too toxic to give IV

why: **AIDS + disseminated cryptococcosis with meningitis and sepsis** = severe disease. **Amphotericin B** (with flucytosine) is the induction regimen, followed by fluconazole.

drug.name: Amphotericin B
drug.use: Cryptococcal meningitis (with flucytosine), mucormycosis, severe invasive fungal infections

stem: A 29-year-old woman has had 24 hours of fever, headache, myalgias and a dry cough during the winter influenza season. Several coworkers are ill. A rapid nasal swab test is positive for influenza B antigen. She has no chronic illnesses and her chest is clear.
oneliner: 29F + 24 h fever, myalgias, dry cough in flu season + rapid test influenza B positive + no comorbidity → best drug?
ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate antiviral therapy?

whyNot.A: **Amantadine**: active only against **influenza A**; this is influenza B
whyNot.D: **Ribavirin**: used for RSV and hepatitis C, not for influenza
whyNot.E: **Azithromycin**: antibacterial, no effect on a viral infection

why: **Acute influenza B within 48 hours of symptoms** is treated with a **neuraminidase inhibitor**, oseltamivir. Amantadine covers only influenza A.

drug.name: Oseltamivir
drug.how: Blocks viral neuraminidase, preventing release of new virions
drug.use: Influenza A and B (treatment and prophylaxis)

stem: A 3-month-old boy born at 28 weeks with chronic lung disease has had 3 days of rhinorrhea, followed by wheezing, tachypnea and nasal flaring. Oxygen saturation is 86% on room air. Nasopharyngeal culture shows fused multinucleated giant cells. Because of his underlying disease, an antiviral is chosen.
oneliner: 3-month-old boy, ex-preterm + chronic lung disease + wheeze, tachypnea, SpO2 86% + culture with multinucleated giant cells → which antiviral?
ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate antiviral drug?

whyNot.C: **Oseltamivir**: influenza A and B, not syncytia-forming RSV
whyNot.E: **Palivizumab**: monoclonal antibody for **prevention** in high-risk infants, not treatment

why: **Bronchiolitis with syncytia in culture in a high-risk infant** = RSV. **Ribavirin** (inhibits IMP dehydrogenase and viral RNA synthesis) is the antiviral for severe disease.

drug.name: Ribavirin
drug.how: Inhibits IMP dehydrogenase and viral RNA polymerase
drug.use: Severe RSV, chronic hepatitis C (with other agents), Lassa fever

stem: A 47-year-old man with asthma who immigrated from Papua New Guinea 8 years ago was started on prednisone 3 weeks ago for an exacerbation. He now has abdominal pain, watery diarrhea, cough and a rapidly moving serpiginous rash on the buttocks. He had unexplained eosinophilia in the past. Sputum shows filariform larvae.
oneliner: 47M + asthma, prednisone for 3 wk + from Papua New Guinea + abdominal pain, diarrhea, cough, moving buttock rash + larvae in sputum → best drug?
ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

whyNot.A: **Praziquantel**: flukes and tapeworms; this is a nematode
whyNot.C: **Hydroxychloroquine**: malaria and autoimmune disease; no activity here
whyNot.D: **Pyrantel**: pinworm, Ascaris and hookworm; not effective for this larval hyperinfection

why: **Steroids unmasking filariform larvae in sputum and larva currens rash after residence in an endemic area** = Strongyloides hyperinfection. Treat with **ivermectin** (older: thiabendazole).

drug.name: Ivermectin
drug.how: Opens glutamate-gated chloride channels, causing paralysis of nematodes and ectoparasites
drug.watch: Mazzotti reaction in onchocerciasis, generally well tolerated

stem: A 15-year-old girl recently immigrated from sub-Saharan Africa after years of swimming in freshwater lakes. She vomited blood this morning. The spleen and liver are enlarged, and there is peripheral eosinophilia. Stool examination shows large eggs with a lateral spine, and endoscopy shows esophageal varices.
oneliner: 15F + immigrant from sub-Saharan Africa, swam in lakes + hematemesis + hepatosplenomegaly, eosinophilia + lateral-spine eggs → best drug?
ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy for the underlying infection?

whyNot.E: **TMP-SMX**: antibacterial and anti-Pneumocystis; not for flukes

why: **Lateral-spine eggs, eosinophilia and portal hypertension after freshwater exposure in Africa** = schistosomiasis (S. mansoni). **Praziquantel** is the drug of choice.

drug.name: Praziquantel
drug.how: Increases tegument calcium permeability, causing spastic paralysis

stem: A 5-year-old girl who attends day care has had nighttime perianal itching for 2 weeks. A cellophane tape applied to the perianal skin in the morning shows colorless, oval eggs flattened on one side. She is otherwise well.
oneliner: 5F + day care + nighttime perianal itch + tape test: eggs flattened on one side → best drug?
ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

whyNot.A: **Metronidazole**: protozoa and anaerobes; this is a nematode
whyNot.D: **Tetracycline**: antibacterial; not for worms, and avoided in young children
whyNot.E: **Praziquantel**: flukes and tapeworms, not this roundworm

why: **Nocturnal anal itching and tape-test eggs** = pinworm (Enterobius). **Mebendazole** inhibits microtubules in the worm and treats pinworm (pyrantel is an alternative).

drug.name: Mebendazole
drug.watch: Abdominal pain, diarrhea; teratogenic (avoid in pregnancy)

stem: A 37-year-old woman who works as a nurse has a deep needlestick injury one hour ago from a patient known to have HIV, whose viral load is unknown. She is HIV-negative on baseline testing and takes no medicines.
oneliner: 37F nurse + deep needlestick from HIV-positive patient 1 hour ago + source viral load unknown + baseline HIV-negative → which management?
ask: Which management is most appropriate now?

whyNot.A: A **single drug** does not give adequate protection; current regimens use **three agents**
whyNot.B: **Delay** wastes the window; prophylaxis works best **within hours** of exposure and starts before any follow-up test
whyNot.C: Covers **hepatitis B**, not HIV; the exposure is to **HIV**
whyNot.D: A **single dose** is no longer used; a full **28-day, three-drug** course is needed

why: After a high-risk exposure, **postexposure prophylaxis** starts **as soon as possible** (ideally within hours, up to 72) with **tenofovir, emtricitabine and an integrase inhibitor** such as dolutegravir or raltegravir, for **28 days**.

drug.name: Tenofovir plus emtricitabine plus dolutegravir
drug.class: Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors plus an integrase strand transfer inhibitor
drug.how: NRTIs terminate viral DNA chains; the integrase inhibitor blocks integration of viral DNA into host DNA
drug.watch: Tenofovir: renal toxicity, bone loss; emtricitabine: skin hyperpigmentation; dolutegravir: insomnia, weight gain

idea.rule: Postexposure prophylaxis is three drugs, started early, for 28 days.
also: Test HIV at baseline and follow up
Hepatitis B and C status of the source also checked
Pre-exposure prophylaxis uses tenofovir plus emtricitabine
